Bachti Alisjahbana | academic_advisors = | doctoral_students = | notable_students = | known_for = | influences = | influenced = | awards = }} }} '''Ayesha Jennifer Verrall''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|aɪ|ʃ|ə}} {{respell|EYE|shə}};{{cite web |title=New Labour MP Dr Ayesha Verrall straight into Cabinet |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dhpTbHO_eNk |website=YouTube | date=November 2020 |publisher=[[RNZ]] |access-date=11 August 2021}} born 1979{{cite news|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300154270/election-2020-jacinda-ardern-no-longer-the-youngest-person-in-her-cabinet-as-average-age-shifts-down|title=Election 2020: Jacinda Ardern no longer the youngest person in her Cabinet, as average age shifts down|first=Henry|last=Cooke|work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=2020-11-10|access-date=2021-10-29}}) is a New Zealand politician, [[Infectious disease (medical specialty)|infectious-diseases]] physician and researcher with expertise in [[tuberculosis]] and [[international health]]. Since 2020, she has been a [[New Zealand House of Representatives|Member of the New Zealand House of Representatives]] for the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]]. Verrall was previously a senior lecturer in pathology and molecular medicine at the [[University of Otago]]. She came to public attention during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in New Zealand|COVID-19 pandemic]] when, after criticising the [[New Zealand government response to the COVID-19 pandemic|Government's pandemic response]], she was commissioned to audit the contact tracing system. Soon after, she was elected to Parliament and appointed to the [[Cabinet of New Zealand|Cabinet]]. She served as [[Minister for Food Safety]], [[Minister for Research, Science and Innovation]], [[Minister for Seniors]], and [[Minister of Health (New Zealand)|Minister of Health]] in the Sixth Labour Government. == Early life and education == Verrall was born in [[Invercargill]] to Lathee and Bill Verrall. She was raised in [[Te Anau]]. Her mother was born in the [[Maldives]] and was the first Maldivian to pass Cambridge examinations in English and study in New Zealand on a [[Colombo Plan]] scholarship.{{Cite news |url= https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/campus/university-of-otago/%E2%80%98reason-hope%E2%80%99-face-workplace-bullying |title='Reason to hope' in face of workplace named after her grandmother, who died when Lathee was two years old.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/121229439/the-story-behind-the-doctor-pushing-for-better-covid19-contact-tracing|title=The story behind the doctor pushing for better Covid-19 contact tracing|last=Macdonald|first=Nikki|date=2020-04-25|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en|access-date=2020-04-25}} In 1997, she was a member of the [[New Zealand Youth Parliament]], selected secondary education at [[Fiordland College]],{{Cite news |date=28 November 2020 |title=Minister reflects on journey a month into her new job |url=https://www.odt.co.nz/regions/southland/minister-reflects-journey-month-her-new-job |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=[[Otago Daily Times]]}} Verrall obtained a [[Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery|Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB)]] in 2004 from the [[University of Otago Dunedin School of Medicine]].{{Cite web |url= https://www.otago.ac.nz/careers/otago067425.html|title=Ayesha Verrall|website=Career Development Centre {{!}} otago.ac.nz|access-date=2020-04-21}} She became the president of the [[Otago University Students' Association]] in 2001. While in this role she lobbied for interest-free student loans. In 2003, Verall led the formation of the ''New Zealand Medical Student Journal'' (NZMSJ).{{Cite web |url= http://www.nzmsj.com/history.html|title=History|website=New Zealand Medical Student Journal|language=en|access-date=2020-04-22}} During the next decade, Verrall trained in [[tropical medicine]], [[bioethics]] and [[international health]] in the United Kingdom, Singapore, and Peru.{{Cite news |url= https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/graduate-funded-tb-study |title=Graduate funded for Tb study|last=Gibb|first=John|date=2012-11-28|work=[[Otago Daily Times]] |language=en|access-date=2020-04-21}} She graduated with a [[Master of Science]] from the [[London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine]] and a Diploma in Tropical Medicine and Hygiene from the [[University of Alabama]] through the [[Instituto Conmemorativo Gorgas de Estudios de la Salud|Gorgas Institute]] in [[Lima|Lima, Peru]].{{Cite web|url= https://www.otago.ac.nz/healthsciences/expertise/Profile/index.html?id=1377|title=Dr Ayesha Verrall {{!}} Division of Health Sciences|website=otago.ac.nz|access-date=2020-04-21}}{{Cite web |url= https://www.otago.ac.nz/internationalhealth/otago661680.html|title=Dr Ayesha Verrall {{!}} Centre for International Health|website=otago.ac.nz|date=4 September 2017 |access-date=2020-04-21}} In 2018, Verrall completed her [[PhD]] in [[Epidemiology of tuberculosis|tuberculosis epidemiology]] at the University of Otago, in collaboration with [[Padjadjaran University]] in [[Indonesia]] and [[Radboud University Nijmegen]] in the [[Netherlands]]. Her research investigated the early clearance immune response to the ''[[Mycobacterium tuberculosis]]'' infection among Indonesian people who were highly exposed to the bacteria yet remained uninfected.{{cite thesis |last=Verrall |first=Ayesha |year=2018 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=Innate Factors in Early Clearance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis |publisher=OUR Archive, University of Otago |hdl=10523/7999 |url=https://ourarchive.otago.ac.nz/handle/10523/7999}} She developed the Innate Factors in Early Clearance of M. tuberculosis (INFECT) cohort as part of her dissertation.{{Cite book|last1=Welasari|first1=Welasari|last2=Suwaryo|first2=Utang|last3=Agustino|first3=Leo|last4=Sulaeman|first4=Affan|chapter=Recruitment and Selection of Head Department (In West Java Province's Government of Indonesia) |date=2020-03-27|title=International Conference on Social Sciences|pages=11–20|publisher=The International Institute of Knowledge Management|doi=10.17501/2357268x.2019.6102|isbn=978-955-3605-36-8|doi-access=free}} == Professional career == Before entering national politics, Verrall was a senior lecturer at the [[University of Otago]] in the Department of Pathology and Molecular Medicine. She taught microbiology to medical students and researched tuberculosis epidemiology, immunology, and host-pathogen interactions. She was also an infectious diseases physician at the [[Capital and Coast District Health Board]] in [[Wellington]] and became an elected member of its board in the [[2019 New Zealand local elections|2019 local elections]]. She stood representing the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] and was appointed as the board's deputy chair.{{cite web |date=7 December 2019 |title=DHB appointments by region |url=https://www.beehive.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2019-12/DHB%20Appointments%20by%20region.pdf |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=Beehive.govt.nz}}{{Cite web |title=CCDHB Board Members |url=https://www.ccdhb.org.nz/about-us/our-board/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200517080627/https://www.ccdhb.org.nz/about-us/our-board/ |archive-date=17 May 2020 |website=ccdhb.org.nz}} During the [[2019–2020 New Zealand measles outbreak]], Verrall advocated for a more strategic approach to allocating government resources to increase vaccination rates for measles and prevent future outbreaks.{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/112695463/concerted-effort-needed-to-increase-measles-vaccinations-and-prevent-further-outbreaks--expert|title=Concerted effort needed to increase measles vaccinations and prevent further outbreaks – expert|last=Macandrew|first=Ruby|date=2019-05-14|website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en|access-date=2020-04-22}} In March 2020, during the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], Verrall called for the government to urgently improve its data on the community spread of [[COVID-19]] by expanding the testing criteria beyond sick people and increasing laboratory testing and contact tracing capabilities to reach 1000 people per day. At the time, contact tracing was only carried out for 50 cases per day.{{Cite web |date=2020-03-25 |title=Location rules out nurse's bid to join contact tracing team
